name: Oganesson

discovery.discoverer: Joint Russian-American team, Dubna & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, and only a handful of atoms have ever been detected.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research at the very edge of the current periodic table
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive with an extremely short half-life (under a millisecond); never produced beyond single atoms.
notableCharacteristics: Named after physicist Yuri Oganessian, one of the most prolific superheavy-element discoverers alive — and, unusually for a noble gas, it's theoretically predicted to be a solid at room temperature rather than a gas, due to extreme relativistic effects.
ncertRelevance: heaviest element on the current periodic table
predicted solid noble gas, breaking the group's usual pattern
whyHere: Relativistic effects are so extreme at this atomic mass that oganesson's outer electrons are predicted to behave unusually reactively for a noble gas, and its atoms are expected to bind together strongly enough to form a solid at room temperature — a genuinely paradigm-breaking prediction for what's nominally Group 18.
didYouKnow: Oganesson is the only element named after a person who was alive at the time of naming and directly involved in its own discovery — a distinction unlikely to be repeated for whichever element comes next.
genZNote: The heaviest element we've got, predicted to be a weird reactive solid instead of a chill noble gas. Group 18's biggest plot twist, quite literally at the edge of the map.
